source: WHO Consolidated Guidelines on TB, Module 2, 2021
text: Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It most commonly affects the lungs (pulmonary TB) and is spread through the air when a person with active pulmonary TB coughs, sneezes, or spits. A person needs to inhale only a few of these germs to become infected. About one-quarter of the global population is estimated to have been infected with TB bacteria, but most people will not go on to develop TB disease.

provenance.source_document: WHO Consolidated Guidelines on TB, Module 2, 2021
provenance.note: Paraphrased for CHW decision support; not a verbatim WHO excerpt.

source: WHO TB Fact Sheet, 2024
text: Common symptoms of active pulmonary TB include a persistent cough (sometimes with blood or sputum), chest pain, weakness, fatigue, weight loss, fever, and night sweats. A cough lasting more than 2-3 weeks is a key indicator that should prompt investigation for TB, especially in high-burden settings.

provenance.source_document: WHO TB Fact Sheet, 2024
provenance.note: Paraphrased for CHW decision support; not a verbatim WHO excerpt.

source: WHO Consolidated Guidelines on TB, Module 2, 2021
text: Computer-aided detection (CAD) software for TB screening on chest X-rays has shown sensitivity comparable to human readers. CAD systems provide a probability score indicating the likelihood of TB-related abnormalities. These are screening tools — a positive screening result must always be followed by confirmatory bacteriological testing such as sputum smear microscopy, Xpert MTB/RIF, or culture.

provenance.source_document: WHO Consolidated Guidelines on TB, Module 2, 2021
provenance.note: Paraphrased for CHW decision support; not a verbatim WHO excerpt.

source: WHO Operational Handbook on TB, Module 2, 2021
text: When interpreting CAD screening results, a higher probability score indicates greater likelihood of TB-related abnormalities on the chest X-ray. However, the threshold for referral should be determined based on the local context, prevalence, and available confirmatory testing. No CAD system replaces the need for bacteriological confirmation of TB disease.

provenance.source_document: WHO Operational Handbook on TB, Module 2, 2021
provenance.note: Paraphrased for CHW decision support; not a verbatim WHO excerpt.

source: WHO Consolidated Guidelines on TB, Module 2, 2021
text: Patients with a positive TB screening result (high probability on CAD or abnormal chest X-ray) should be referred for confirmatory diagnostic testing. The recommended first-line confirmatory test is Xpert MTB/RIF, which simultaneously detects TB and rifampicin resistance. Where Xpert is unavailable, sputum smear microscopy should be performed. Referral should be prompt — delays in diagnosis increase transmission risk.

provenance.source_document: WHO Consolidated Guidelines on TB, Module 2, 2021
provenance.note: Paraphrased for CHW decision support; not a verbatim WHO excerpt.

source: WHO Operational Handbook on TB, Module 2, 2021
text: For patients with an indeterminate or borderline screening result, clinical judgement is needed. If symptoms persist (cough > 2 weeks, weight loss, night sweats), repeat the chest X-ray or proceed directly to sputum testing. If the patient is asymptomatic with a borderline result, schedule a follow-up screening in 2-4 weeks. Document the result and ensure the patient returns for follow-up.

provenance.source_document: WHO Operational Handbook on TB, Module 2, 2021
provenance.note: Paraphrased for CHW decision support; not a verbatim WHO excerpt.

source: WHO Operational Handbook on TB, Module 2, 2021
text: A negative screening result (low probability on CAD, normal chest X-ray) in an asymptomatic person suggests TB disease is unlikely at this time. However, advise the patient to return if they develop symptoms such as persistent cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats. In high-burden settings, periodic screening may be recommended for high-risk groups including people living with HIV, household contacts of TB patients, and healthcare workers.

provenance.source_document: WHO Operational Handbook on TB, Module 2, 2021
provenance.note: Paraphrased for CHW decision support; not a verbatim WHO excerpt.

source: WHO Consolidated Guidelines on TB, Module 4, 2022
text: Drug-susceptible pulmonary TB is treated with a standard 6-month regimen: 2 months of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol (intensive phase), followed by 4 months of isoniazid and rifampicin (continuation phase). Treatment must be completed in full even if the patient feels better — incomplete treatment is a major driver of drug resistance. Directly observed therapy (DOT) is recommended to ensure adherence.

provenance.source_document: WHO Consolidated Guidelines on TB, Module 4, 2022
provenance.note: Paraphrased for CHW decision support; not a verbatim WHO excerpt.

source: WHO Patient Education Materials, 2023
text: TB is curable. With proper treatment, most people with TB recover fully. Treatment takes 6 months — it is important to take all medicines as prescribed, even after feeling better. Stopping treatment early can cause the disease to return in a drug-resistant form that is harder to treat. During treatment, cover your mouth when coughing, ensure good ventilation, and attend all follow-up appointments.

provenance.source_document: WHO Patient Education Materials, 2023
provenance.note: Paraphrased for CHW decision support; not a verbatim WHO excerpt.

source: WHO Patient Education Materials, 2023
text: A positive screening result does not mean you definitely have TB — it means further testing is needed. The screening uses artificial intelligence to check your chest X-ray for signs that could indicate TB. If additional tests confirm TB, treatment will be started. TB treatment is free in most countries through national TB programmes. Early detection and treatment save lives and prevent spread to family and community members.

provenance.source_document: WHO Patient Education Materials, 2023
provenance.note: Paraphrased for CHW decision support; not a verbatim WHO excerpt.

source: WHO Consolidated Guidelines on TB, Module 1, 2022
text: People living with HIV are at significantly higher risk of developing TB disease. TB is the leading cause of death among people with HIV. All people living with HIV should be regularly screened for TB. If TB is diagnosed, treatment should start immediately alongside antiretroviral therapy. TB preventive treatment (TPT) is recommended for people with HIV who do not have active TB.

provenance.source_document: WHO Consolidated Guidelines on TB, Module 1, 2022
provenance.note: Paraphrased for CHW decision support; not a verbatim WHO excerpt.

source: WHO TB Infection Prevention and Control, 2019
text: To reduce TB transmission in healthcare facilities: ensure adequate natural ventilation, implement cough etiquette (cover mouth when coughing), separate patients with suspected TB from others, use personal protective equipment (N95 respirators) when caring for TB patients, and minimize time spent in enclosed spaces with suspected TB patients. Early diagnosis and treatment initiation are the most effective infection control measures.

provenance.source_document: WHO TB Infection Prevention and Control, 2019
provenance.note: Paraphrased for CHW decision support; not a verbatim WHO excerpt.

source: WHO Consolidated Guidelines on TB, Module 5, 2022
text: TB in children can be difficult to diagnose because children often cannot produce sputum and the disease may present differently than in adults. Chest X-ray screening combined with clinical assessment is particularly important for childhood TB. Children who are household contacts of a TB patient should be evaluated and may be candidates for TB preventive treatment. A shorter 4-month treatment regimen is now recommended for children with non-severe TB.

provenance.source_document: WHO Consolidated Guidelines on TB, Module 5, 2022
provenance.note: Paraphrased for CHW decision support; not a verbatim WHO excerpt.

source: WHO Consolidated Guidelines on TB, Module 2, 2021
text: Ètò àyẹ̀wò kọ̀mpútà (CAD) fún àyẹ̀wò ikọ́ fée fée (TB) lára àwọn fọ́tò àyà (X-ray) ti fi hàn pé ó wúlò tó ti ènìyàn.

source: WHO Consolidated Guidelines on TB, Module 2, 2021
text: Ní láti ṣe àwọn àyẹ̀wò bíi Xpert MTB/RIF tàbí microscopic sputum test fìdí rẹ̀ múlẹ̀.

text: Àwọn aláìsàn tí àyẹ̀wò wọn bá fi hàn pé wọ́n ní TB (gíga lórí CAD tàbí fọ́tò àyà) yẹ kí a tọ́ka wọn lọ fún àyẹ̀wò ìdánilójú.

source: WHO Consolidated Guidelines on TB, Module 2, 2021

source: WHO Operational Handbook on TB, Module 2, 2021
text: Fún àwọn aláìsàn tí àyẹ̀wò wọn kò daju, ìpinnu dókítà ṣe kókó. Tí àmì àrùn bá tẹ̀síwájú (ikọ́ > ọ̀sẹ̀ méjì), tún X-ray ṣe.

source: WHO Operational Handbook on TB, Module 2, 2021
text: Ṣètò àyẹ̀wò mìíràn ní ọ̀sẹ̀ 2 sí 4. Rí i pé aláìsàn padà wá fún àyẹ̀wò mìíràn.

source: WHO Operational Handbook on TB, Module 2, 2021
text: Sọ fún aláìsàn láti padà wá tí ó bá ní àmì àrùn bíi ikọ́ gígùn, ibà, dídínwúwó, tàbí òógùn òru.

source: WHO Patient Education Materials, 2023
text: TB ṣeé wòsàn pẹ̀lú ìtọ́jú tó tọ́, ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ̀ ènìyàn ni ara wọn ń yá padà. Ìtọ́jú náà ń gba oṣù 6.

source: WHO Patient Education Materials, 2023

text: Àbájáde àyẹ̀wò tó fi hàn pé ó ṣeé ṣe kò túmọ̀ sí pé o ní TB dandan. Ní láti ṣe àwọn àyẹ̀wò sputum sí i.

text: Tí àyẹ̀wò mìíràn bá fìdí rẹ̀ múlẹ̀, ìtọ́jú yóò bẹ̀rẹ̀ kánkán. Ìtọ́jú TB jẹ́ ọ̀fẹ́ ní ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ̀ orílẹ̀-èdè.

source: WHO Consolidated Guidelines on TB, Module 2, 2021
text: Kwamfuta mai taimaka wa tantancewa (CAD) don tantance cutar TB a hoton kirji (X-ray) ta nuna ƙwazo kwatankwacin na kwararru.

text: Ngwaọrụ kọmputa (CAD) maka nyocha TB na chest X-ray na-egosi ike yiri nke mmadụ. Nyocha dị mma chọrọ nyocha nkwenye ọzọ.
